stations.name: Expedition
stations.title: Investigation Crater
intro: A huge round hole in the ground with steep rocky walls. Scientists come here to study how space affects the human body, and to find ways to treat and prevent the problems. The goal is to make space travel safer.
Missions to the Moon and Mars are longer, and that brings more risks:

list: Longer delays when talking to Earth.
Less help from Earth with food, supplies, and emergency medical care.

prompt: The science team has been measuring radiation in the crater. Mars has a thin atmosphere, so much more radiation reaches the ground than on Earth. The detectors hold the data scientists need to keep astronauts safe, but their batteries are almost empty.
Your radiation suit is back at the base. Going to get it takes time, and the detectors keep running down.
How do you do the expedition?

options.label: Go back for the suit and stay longer

base.text: You work for hours with your suit on. The detectors collect a good amount of data. The suit blocks part of the radiation, but not all of it, and your health drops a little.
You stay out without the shield until every detector has finished.

branches.text: The radiation is far stronger than your body can take. Your legs give out, and the team carries you back to the base. The doctors do everything they can, but it's too late. You don't survive.

otherwise.text: You bring back all the data, but the radiation leaves you weak and dizzy. You were lucky this time.

science.text: Missions to the Moon and Mars mean more time in weightlessness, more radiation exposure, longer communication delays with Earth, and less ability to rely on Earth for food, materials and emergency medical help. Scientists study these risks to make space travel safer.

source.title: Why do we conduct science experiments in space?

stations.name: Greenhouse
stations.title: Greenhouse
intro: A long room with plants growing under bright purple lights. There's lettuce, potatoes, and radishes in trays, with pipes that carry water to each row.
This is where the crew gets its fresh food. It is the only place on the base where food can grow.
stations.doneText: The greenhouse is stable for now.
prompt: The panel shows three readings drifting: temperature, humidity, and lighting.
You can set all three right, but it would use most of the energy you have left. If the conditions are not right, it could harm the harvest.

options.label: Control all three. It uses a lot of energy.

base.text: All the settings are perfect, but it uses a lot of energy. The plants keep growing and the harvest is great.

options.label: Fix the temperature and the lighting.

base.text: The temperature and lights are set, but the humidity is still off and the air stays too damp.

branches.text: By evening there's mold on one of the trays. You have to throw out the whole tray.

otherwise.text: The plants handled the extra moisture. Nothing grew on them this time, but the risk is still there.

options.label: Fix the humidity and the lighting.

base.text: The humidity and lights are set, but the heater shuts down overnight to save energy, and the room gets colder.

branches.text: The cold slows the plants down. They stop growing, and the harvest will be much smaller.

otherwise.text: The plants made it through the cold. They look a little pale, but they're alive.

science.text: Growing food in space needs a controlled environment close to what plants are used to on Earth. In the Advanced Plant Habitat, the temperature, humidity and lighting are all kept under control.

stations.name: Habitat
stations.title: Habitat
intro: This is where the crew lives and sleeps. It's a sealed building with bunks, a small kitchen, and a control panel for air and power.
Along the back wall are the systems that keep everyone alive: the heating and air equipment, the computers, and the radio and navigation gear. They all need regular maintenance.
stations.doneText: The maintenance is done for today.
prompt: The panel shows three systems due for service: temperature and life support, the computer network, and communication and navigation.
Servicing everything uses a lot of energy. A system that isn't serviced might fail, and a failure in any of them could put the whole base at risk.

base.text: You spend the afternoon checking every system, changing filters, and updating the computers. Everything passes.
You service the heating and air systems. They're ready to run.

branches.text: That night the computer network crashes. The control panel goes blank, and the crew has to run the base by hand until it's rebooted.
Communication and navigation go down. The base can't reach Earth, and the rover can't find its way back until it's fixed.

otherwise.text: Nothing else breaks this time. The other systems are still overdue for service.

base.text: You leave the maintenance for later.

branches.text: The heating and air system stops. The temperature drops and the air gets stale. The crew works through the night to restart it. A failure like this could cost the whole base.
The computer network crashes. The control panel goes blank, and the crew has to run the base by hand until it's rebooted.
Communication and navigation go down. The base can't reach Earth, and the rover can't find its way back until it's fixed.

otherwise.text: Nothing breaks this time. The systems still need service, and the risk is still there.

science.text: Maintenance takes up a big part of an astronaut's time and energy on the space station. If it is not done, the thermoregulation and survival systems, the computer networks, or the communication and navigation equipment can fail. A failure in any one of them can be very serious.

stations.name: Solar Panels
stations.title: Solar Panels
intro: Rows of flat panels face the Sun. They turn sunlight into the power the whole base runs on.
Mars is dusty, and the wind blows red dust onto the panels all the time.
stations.alarm: An alarm goes off at the control box. A solar storm is heading for the base.
stations.doneText: The panels are quiet now. The storm is over.
prompt: A solar storm is coming. It could last a few hours or the whole night. Strong bursts from the Sun can damage electronics. If all the energy is turned off, the lights, the heat, and the radio will stop working.

base.text: You turned everything off. The base stayed dark and cold all night, and the food in the freezer spoiled.

branches.text: A small surge still reached the base, and one machine stopped working.

otherwise.text: The equipment came through the storm fine.

branches.text: The storm hits hard. A power surge runs through the base, and some of the equipment burns out.

otherwise.text: The storm passes without hitting the base. Everything keeps working, and the equipment is fine.

base.text: You shut down the science instruments and kept the essentials on. Tonight's data is lost.

branches.text: A small surge still got through, and one machine stopped working.

science.text: Sometimes the Sun unleashes a massive explosion that sends very fast-moving particles toward Mars. We call this a solar storm. In September 2017 one reached Mars and lit up an aurora 25 times brighter than normal. Radiation on the ground was twice as high as any earlier measurement.

source.title: Large Solar Storm Sparks Global Aurora and Doubles Radiation Levels on the Martian Surface

stations.name: Robot Garage
stations.title: Robot Garage
intro: Two machines live here: a long robotic arm and a smaller robot with two hands for delicate jobs. On the space station, the real ones are called Canadarm2 and Dextre.

A robot job isn't just pressing a button. The team has to line up the robot's work with the base's other systems, like communications, electricity, and computers. They plan where the cameras go and what path the arm will follow. They also check which software updates are needed and look for problems ahead of time. Engineers on the support team help at every step.
stations.doneText: The robots are ready for tomorrow.
prompt: Tomorrow the arm has to move a heavy part to the solar panels. Three jobs need to be done first: coordinate with the base's other systems, plan the cameras and the arm's path, and update the software and look for problems.
There's time and energy to do all three, but it will use a lot of energy.

options.label: Do all three jobs. The robot is fully ready.

base.text: You spend the day on every step. The systems are lined up, the cameras are placed, and the software is up to date. The arm moves the part without a problem. The base is low on energy tonight.

options.label: Coordinate the systems and plan the path, but skip the software update.

base.text: The systems are lined up and the arm's path is planned.

branches.text: Halfway through the job, the robot's software freezes. The arm stops in the middle of the move, and you have to restart it before it can finish.

otherwise.text: The old software held up this time. It's still overdue for an update.

options.label: Plan the path and update the software, but skip the coordination.

base.text: The path is planned and the software is up to date.

branches.text: When the arm starts moving, it pulls a lot of power. The radio and the lights go out for a while, because nobody planned for it.

otherwise.text: The power held up this time. Nobody checked how the arm would affect the other systems.

science.text: A robotics operation needs a whole team: they coordinate the robots with the communications, electrical and computer systems, plan the camera positions and the robot's path, prepare software updates and look for possible problems. Engineering support helps the whole way.

stations.name: Spaceship
stations.title: Spaceship
intro: The ship that brought the crew to Mars. It landed at the edge of the base and hasn't moved since.
Inside there's a cockpit with screens and controls, a small cargo bay, and the seats the crew strapped into during the trip. Most of the equipment is turned off to save power.

laboratory.name: Laboratory
laboratory.title: Investigation Lab
intro: A sealed tent with white tables and a computer that analyzes data. Labs like this let scientists use the unique conditions of space to run experiments that prepare us for deep-space trips. What they learn also helps improve life on Earth.
To open the lab you need two things: data to analyze and energy to run the equipment. The results get sent to Earth.

options.label: Analyze it fast. It uses little energy, but there's a 10% chance something goes wrong and you lose all the data.

branches.text: Halfway through, the analyzer crashes and wipes the files. All the data is gone, and there's no way to get it back.

otherwise.text: The quick analysis works. You send the results to Earth.

options.label: Analyze it carefully. It uses a lot of energy, but you get all the data.

base.text: You run the full analysis. It takes a lot of energy, but every piece of data is checked and nothing is lost. You send the results to Earth.

science.text: Labs in space let scientists use the unique conditions of space for experiments. They have two goals: preparing for trips to deep-space destinations, and improving the quality of life on Earth.

source.title: Why do we conduct science experiments in space?
